messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kiran Patel, a 24‑year‑old painter of South‑Eastern Asian heritage, began canvasing fresh murals on the gallery wall when his world turned sideways. A few months earlier, his girlfriend had pushed him hard enough that a bruised cheek and a sudden, electric fear became the first page of a trauma diary he never intended to keep. The night she slammed the door and slammed his head into the table, he fled, swearing that the sound of the house creaking at night would always echo his nightmare. Ever since, Kiran reports intrusive thoughts of that night that come unbidden, an ever‑present uncertainty about his safety, and a chronic sense that somebody is watching him even when he is alone in his studio. Those intrusive thoughts and that feeling of being watched have driven Kiran to develop a host of coping strategies. He refuses to go to bed unless he can turn the lights on, and when he tries to sleep he freezes at the first rustle of a chair. The fear of the unseen has also pushed him to avoid any place or time that might remind him of the assault; he keeps his tools in a locked chest and avoids the subway during rush hour. The very act of entering a room triggers an automatic scan for exits, a habit that has become his default every time he steps into a new space. When a thought surfaces, a flood of the assault’s image rushes through him, making the memory feel vivid and unending. Kiran’s internal narrative is steeped in self‑blame. He insists the night’s violence happened because of the “kind of person” he is, and this belief magnifies his sense of threat: he feels that any corner could conceal an imminent danger. The shame of being perceived as weak fuels the intrusive thoughts, which feel like constant surveillance. His guilt also paints the memory of that night as more relentless, as if the violence never truly stopped, making his sense of inadequacy grow sharper each time he recalls it. Whenever Kiran brings the assault to mind, the sudden clarity of the blow intermingles with the gaps in his timeline, and a surge of panic takes hold. The fragmented recollection feeds his conviction that he is still trapped and unworthy, reinforcing the belief that he belongs nowhere. The recollection also triggers the sensation that everyday noises could be the attacker returning, making ordinary sounds feel like looming threats. That heightened sense of danger forces him to freeze, to keep from dreaming, and to shun anything that might remind him of the attacker. The constant scanning and sense that a threat lingers in every hallway drive Kiran to avoid dreaming entirely. The relentless alertness forces him to replay the assault in his mind, reinforcing the memory with each rehearsal. He becomes convinced that his perceived inadequacy is real, that he can never feel safe. The ever‑present danger amplifies the intrusive thoughts that come as if someone is watching him, even in silence. By staying away from any dream, by freezing whenever a spark of fear ignites, Kiran never processes the event, keeping the memory fragmented. The avoidance also cements his belief that he is fundamentally flawed. Each time he evades a reminder, the urge to stay vigilant strengthens, making the intrusive thoughts feel even more intrusive. The avoidance also heightens his threat perception, making him scan even the quietest corners. Today Kiran sits before his easel, brush poised but trembling, feeling the weight of every brushstroke as a test of his vigilance. He finally seeks help because the cycle has grown too tight: he cannot sleep, he fears being watched in his own apartment, and he longs for a way to regain control over his mind and his life.
